problem: Prior learned navigation behaviors/skills are discrete, short-horizon and assume simple dynamics or fully observable states, so they cannot encode complex long-horizon trajectories. Behavior-less visual memory (dense images/features, SLAM) is memory-hungry.
motivation: Robots repeating navigation routines need compact visual memory for path following and sparse topological maps. Learning continuous behavior embeddings from egocentric visual demonstrations could give memory-efficient, robust, composable navigation without SLAM.
key_idea: Encode a visual demonstration sequence into a 32-d continuous embedding with an LSTM encoder, and decode it with a closed-loop waypoint generator plus attractor (start/end image) features, segmenting long paths into composable behaviors.
insight: The embedding space implicitly learns visual odometry (t-SNE shows a smooth manifold of length and turning direction), which explains generalization to unseen environments. Ablations show removing the attractor network hurts most on multi-behavior following (initial misalignment and switching), and removing the embedding degrades single-behavior performance sharply. Choice-point-based segmentation is necessary for linking demonstrations: without it, map connectivity shows almost no generalization.
method: Behavior encoder: CNN over consecutive image pairs feeds an LSTM; the final state z_{T-1} is a 32-d embedding of the demonstration (variable length).

Waypoint generator: LSTM conditioned on z_D, the embedding z'_t of the executed images so far, and attractor features; outputs the next local waypoint (x,y) and progress phi_t, fed to an RMP/PID low-level controller.
Attractor network: CNN relating current observation to the first and last demo images (800-dim features) to align the start and detect the goal.
Behavior segmentation and switching: long paths are split into equally spaced segments of at most K observations, adjacent segments share attractors, and the robot switches when phi>=0.95.

Choice-point composition: a classifier predicts next-waypoint direction (128 bins); peaks in directional variance mark intersections/doorways, giving consistent attractors for linking demonstrations into topological maps (Dijkstra planning).
Training: 100k trajectories from 18 Gibson scenes, waypoint and progress regression with DAgger and initial pose jitter.

setting.backbone: CNN + LSTM encoder and waypoint generator (trained from scratch), with RMP laser-based low-level controller
setting.training_data: 100k trajectories from 18 large Gibson environments (laser RMP controller following A* waypoints) plus DAgger rollouts; 5 epochs of 200k samples
setting.observation: egocentric 64x64 RGB, 120° FOV (laser used only by low-level controller for obstacle avoidance)
setting.action_space: predicted continuous relative waypoints executed by a low-level controller (velocity/steering) on a non-holonomic car
setting.privileged: none at test time for the policy (demonstration images given); low-level controller uses laser scans; GT poses used only for training supervision

numbers.eval_set_note: 500 long trajectories (avg 20 m) across 5 unseen large Gibson environments
numbers.extra: avg memory 19 KB per trajectory: 6 attractors + 32-float embeddings; initial pose jitter
numbers.evidence: Table 1: Comparing memory efficiency and success rate (SR) of different methods for long-horizon visual path following
Table 2: Comparing sizes of topological maps and planning success rates

numbers_note: Single-behavior success curves, ablations and compression-ratio plots are only in figures; the >95% SR up to 128 steps is stated in text. Obstacle-robustness table: 78.8/82.6/85.1/89.0% success at offsets 0/0.075/0.15/0.225 m.
results: CBE follows ~20 m paths with 97.2% SR using 19 KB, versus SLAM 1024x1024 at 96.3% with 341 KB and SLC at 93.7% with 1548 KB (>10x memory savings). Topological maps are ~30x smaller in storage than SLC (1.2–2.0 MB vs 36–65 MB) with similar or higher planning SR.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation (Gibson); no real robot, and training was without obstacles.
A single embedding degrades beyond ~128 steps and fixed-distance segmentation is needed; the choice-point method leaves a connectivity gap to dense maps.
Relies on a laser-based low-level controller for obstacle avoidance.
builds_on: SLC (Meng et al. 2019 scaling local control)
